Bulk work is better served by an AFTER statement trigger with transition tables, or a loader-written summary. Recursion is avoided by never auditing the audit table and by scoping triggers. Permissions on the audit table must be restricted to the owner. The explicit trade-off, failing the transaction when the audit write fails, is the reliability choice the prompt asks for, with the cost of availability.

citations.quote: A trigger that is marked FOR EACH ROW is called once for every row that the operation modifies.

The REFERENCING option enables collection of transition relations , which are row sets that include all of the rows inserted, deleted, or modified by the current SQL statement. This feature lets the trigger see a global view of what the statement did, not just one row at a time.

One can disable or enable a single trigger specified by name, or all triggers on the table, or only user triggers (this option excludes internally generated constraint triggers, such as those that are used to implement foreign key constraints or deferrable uniqueness and exclusion constraints).

Disabling or enabling internally generated constraint triggers requires superuser privileges; it should be done with caution since of course the integrity of the constraint cannot be guaranteed if the triggers are not executed.

questions.notes: Correct. Per-row triggers execute the function once per row, so millions of rows mean millions of calls plus extra statements/index writes. Statement-level transition tables or a staging table applied in one set-based INSERT/MERGE avoid that. ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER (user triggers) can be done by the owner but bypasses integrity and audit; disabling internal constraint triggers needs superuser and forfeits the constraint, so the load must be validated and reconciled afterwards.
